en: And so I shall tell you this story of his; listen: there is a region named Pratiṣṭhāna on the banks of the Godāvarī.
In that place, there was formerly a king named Trivikramasena, the son of Vikramasena, who possessed the prowess of Śakra and was renowned for his fame.
Every day, as that king sat in his assembly hall,
a monk named Kṣāntiśīla would approach him and present a fruit for the sake of service.
The king also, taking that fruit,
gave it every day into the hand of the treasurer who was standing nearby.
When ten years had passed in this manner, on one occasion,
after giving that fruit to the king, the mendicant departed from the assembly hall.
By chance, that king gave the fruit to a young pet monkey that had escaped from the hands of its keepers and entered there.
As that monkey was eating it, from within the fruit,
whose core had split open, there emerged an unsurpassed, priceless jewel.
Seeing that, the king took it and asked the treasurer:
"Those fruits which were brought to me daily by the monk—" *Suttanipāta 12.8.28* (Vetullavāda 0.8).
"Where have you always kept those things that were placed in your hand?
Hearing this, the terrified treasurer replied to him:
"I cast them into the treasury through the window without opening it;
if you command me, O King, I shall open it and search for them."
Having spoken thus and being permitted by the king, the treasury official departed; returning in a moment, he addressed his lord once more.
"I do not see those fruits here in the treasury;
instead, O Lord, I see a heap of jewels ablaze with rays of light."
Having heard that and being pleased with the treasurer for giving those jewels,
the king questioned that monk— who had arrived as before— the following day.
"O monk, why do you serve me every day with such expenditure of wealth?
I will not accept your reward now until you speak."
To the king who had spoken thus, the monk said in private:
"I have a means of mantra-accomplishment that requires the assistance of a hero."
"In this matter, O lord of heroes, I request that you provide assistance.
Having heard that, the king agreed to him, saying, "So be it."
Then that ascetic, being pleased, spoke again to the king:
"In that case, on the coming fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at the arrival of night..."
"O Lord, you must come from here to my presence, as I wait beneath the banyan tree within this great cremation ground."
When the king replied, "Very well, I shall do so," that ascetic Kṣāntiśīla went to his own dwelling, filled with joy.
Then, having reached the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, that Great Being,
remembering the request made by that monk, [acted accordingly].
At twilight, dressed in blue garments and with a crest of *tāla* leaves,
he went forth from the capital at night, sword in hand and unobserved.
And he went toward that place, blackened by a mass of terrible and dense darkness,
its appearance made dreadful by the flames from the fierce eyes of the funeral pyre's fire.
It was crowded with the skeletons, skulls, and bones of countless hell-beings,
and surrounded by exultant, nearby, and terrifying bhūtas and vetālas.
Like another form of Bhairava, deep and terrifying, that cremation ground resounded with the great howling of jackals; yet he remained undaunted.
Having searched for him there and found that monk beneath a banyan tree performing the ritual layout of a mandala, he approached and spoke to him.
"Here I am come, O monk; tell me, what shall I do for you?
Having heard that and seeing the king, the monk spoke to him with joy:
"O King, if you will grant me this favor, then go from here alone toward the south;
after traveling a long distance, there stands a śiṃśapā tree."
There stands a certain man, dead and suspended;
go there, O hero, bring him here, and grant me your protection.
Upon hearing this, that king, true to his promise and a great hero, said, "So be it," and then set out toward the southern direction.
Having gone there by a path marked by blazing funeral pyres amidst the darkness, he somehow reached that śiṃśapā tree.
Upon its shoulder, he saw him hanging down— smelling of raw flesh and scorched by the smoke of the funeral pyre— like a corpse of a spirit suspended from a tree.
Having climbed up there onto that ground, he let go of the severed rope;
and having fallen there, he suddenly cried out in agony as if in pain.
Then, having descended out of compassion and fearing for his life, he touched that limb of the king; by that act, the corpse let out a loud, mocking laugh.
Then that king, perceiving him to be possessed by a vetāla, said without trembling, "Why do you laugh? Come, let us go."
He spoke thus; he did not see the corpse with the vetāla on the ground, but then he saw it again, suspended hanging from that very tree.
Then, having climbed back up, he brought him down once more;
for even from a thunderbolt, the jewel of the mind of heroes remains unbroken.
Then King Trivikramasena, having placed that corpse along with the vetāla upon his shoulder in silence, set out to go.
And as he was walking, the Vetāla situated within the corpse, perched upon his shoulder, said:
"O King, listen; I shall tell you a story to divert you on your journey."
There is a city named Vārāṇasī, the dwelling place of the Enemy of Cities (Śiva),
which, frequented by holy people, is like a plateau of Mount Kailāsa.
The celestial river, constantly situated near her banks and laden with abundant waters,
shines like a string of pearls upon her.
In that city, there was formerly a king named Pratāpamukuṭa, who consumed the forest of his enemies' clans with the fire of his majesty.
He had a son named Vajramukuṭa,
who humbled the pride of the God of Love through his beauty and valor, as well as that of his enemies.
There, that prince had a high-minded minister’s son named Buddhiśarīra, who was his friend and dearer to him than his own body.
Once, while playing with that friend, the prince traveled a long distance on account of his excessive addiction to hunting.
Like the chowries of the glory of his valor, he severed the maned heads of lions with his arrows and entered a great forest.
There, while the cuckoos sang like bards out of season,
the trees rendered service with their clusters of blossoms as flickering chowries.
Followed by that minister’s son, he beheld a lake that was like another ocean, the dwelling place for the birth of various lotuses.
At that very moment, a certain maiden of divine form, accompanied by her retinue, arrived at that lake for the purpose of bathing and was seen by him.
As if filling the lake with a torrent of loveliness,
she seemed to create a new forest of blue lotuses there with her glances.
With her face, which surpassed the moon and seemed to reject the lotuses,
she captivated the mind of that prince at that very moment.
The youth likewise captivated her eyes in such a way that the maiden could no longer perceive even her own modesty or her ornaments.
As he gazed upon that youth along with his followers, wondering, "Who might this be?",
she employed the pretext of playful charm to announce her own name, her country, and other details.
She took a blue lotus from her flower garland and placed it behind her ear;
she fashioned an arrangement of teeth for a long time, and having taken them up, she set them in place.
She placed a lotus on her head and then applied her hand to her heart;
yet at that time, the prince did not understand that sign of hers.
But his wise friend, the minister’s son, perceived this;
and in an instant, that maiden was led away from there by her attendants.
Having reached her own home, she lay upon a couch with her body resting there,
but she fixed her mind upon that prince for the sake of her own mental conception.
That prince, like a Vidyadhara who has lost his magic power,
went to his own city and fell into a state of great misery without her.
Then, questioned in private by that friend, the minister’s son, he—
losing his composure as the boy described her as not difficult to attain— spoke.
"How can she be found whose name, village, and lineage are not even known? Why do you deceive me with such falsehoods?"
Thus addressed by the prince, the minister’s son replied to him:
"Did you not see that which was indicated by her through signs?"
"Because an utpala lotus was placed upon your ear, she said this to you:
'I dwell in the kingdom of King Karṇotpala.'"
"Because she arranged her teeth in such a way, she said this:
'Know me there to be the daughter of a tooth-maker.'"
She who was adorned with lotuses spoke the name "Padmāvatī";
placing her hand upon his heart, she declared, "My life-breaths are in you."
For in the land of Kaliṅga there is a famous king named Karṇotpala; he has a great ivory-carver who is well-known for his skill in craftsmanship.
To him, who is named Saṅgrāmavardhana, there also belongs in the three worlds a maiden named Padmāvatī, a jewel who is dearer to him than his own life.
And this, O King, is known to me exactly as it is from the world;
therefore, I have understood that designation which indicates its region and so forth. (SoKss_12,8.86 [Vet_1.28])
Thus addressed by that minister’s son, the prince was pleased with the wise youth; having found his means, he rejoiced.
Having consulted with him, he set out from his own palace accompanied by that man;
seeking his beloved, he went once more in that direction under the pretext of hunting.
And on the way, having outstripped his army with the speed of wind-swift horses,
he proceeded to the territory of Kaliṅga accompanied only by the minister’s son.
Having reached that city of King Karṇotpala,
they searched for and found the residence of that ivory-carver.
Not far from there, both the minister’s son and the prince entered the house of an elderly woman for the sake of lodging.

Having given the two horses water and fodder and having stationed them in a secure place, while the prince remained there, the minister’s son spoke to that old woman: dattāmbuyavasau vāhau gupte 'vasthāpya cātra saḥ / rājaputre sthite vṛddhāṃ mantriputro jagāda tām // SoKss_12,8.92 (Vet_1.34) //
"Mother, do you know the ivory-carver Saṅgrāmavardhana?
Having heard that, the old woman spoke to him with faith:
"I am indeed her nurse,
and I have now been appointed by him as the senior attendant beside his own daughter, Padmāvatī."
However, I do not always go there with my garments spoiled;
for a wicked son or a gambler, upon seeing my clothes, would indeed steal them.
When she had spoken thus, the minister’s son, being pleased, gratified that old woman there with the gift of his upper garment and other items, and spoke to her again:
"You are our mother; therefore we tell you this: do for us that which is secret.
Go to this Padmāvatī, the daughter of Dantaghāṭa, and speak to her."
"The prince whom you saw at the lake has arrived here;
out of affection, he has sent me to inform you of this."
Having heard that, the old woman, subdued by the Dānava, said "So be it," and having gone to the side of Padmāvatī, she returned a moment later.
When questioned, she said to the prince and the minister’s son:
"Having gone there, I secretly informed her of your arrival."
Having heard this, she rebuked me and struck me on both cheeks with her two hands, which were smeared with camphor.
Then, distressed by this humiliation, I came here weeping;
look, my two sons, at these finger-rings upon my face.
When she had spoken thus, that highly wise son of a minister said to the prince, who was despondent with despair, in private: SoKss_12,8.103 (Vet_1.45) //
"Do not fall into despair; for when she rebuked me while guarding the secret, she struck her ten fingers, white as camphor, against her mouth."
Thus it was said regarding this position: "Wait for these ten nights of the bright fortnight, like those possessed of the moon, until you have become worthy of reunion."
Having thus comforted the prince, the minister’s son then secretly sold some gold he had in his hand at the marketplace.
With that old woman, he prepared a costly meal;
then the two of them ate it together with her.
Having thus spent ten days in this manner, the minister’s son sent that old woman back once more to Padmāvatī for the sake of further inquiry.
She too, being greedy for fine food, drink, and other luxuries, went to her house out of consideration for him; returning once more, she spoke to the two of them.
Having gone from here today, even though I remained there in silence,
she herself again poured out that offense of your conversation.
Struck on this breast by her three fingers, stained with lac,
I have now come here from her presence.
Having heard that, the minister’s son said freely to the prince:
"Do not entertain any other suspicion; for this [ornament] was indeed placed in her heart by her."
Having skillfully applied three finger-marks of lac-dye, she indicated:
"I have remained menstruating for three nights."
Having spoken thus to the prince, when three days had passed,
the minister’s son sent that old woman back once more to Padmāvatī.
She went to her house and was honored and fed by her;
with affectionate games of drinking and other diversions, she spent the day there in amusement.
And as that old woman was wishing to return home in the evening,
a terrifying clamor arose outside at that moment.
"Alas, alas! This intoxicated elephant has broken from its tethering post and is running amok, trampling the people!"—such was the cry heard by the world there.
Then Padmāvatī spoke thus to that old woman:
"It is not proper for you to travel by this road, which is clearly blocked by elephants."
Having placed you upon that platform with its firmly fastened ropes,
we shall cast you down here through this large window.
Then, having climbed a tree in the house garden and leaped over that wall,
descend by another tree and go to your own home.
Having said this, she then had that old woman cast down from the window into the garden by her maidservants using a rope-swing.
Having gone there, he related everything exactly as it had happened along the path described,
to that prince and to the minister’s son.
Then that minister’s son spoke to the prince:
"Your desire is accomplished, for she has shown you the path through her reasoning."
Therefore, go this very day to that place; when the king has departed at this twilight, enter the mansion of your beloved by this very same path.
Thus addressed by him, the prince, accompanied by that old woman, went to that garden by the path along the wall as she had described.
There he saw that rope hanging down with its seat,
attended from above by maidservants who were looking out for the path.
As soon as he saw her mounted there, he was quickly hoisted up by those maidservants through the window by means of a rope and entered the presence of his beloved.
When he had entered, the minister’s son went to his own abode;
but the prince beheld Padmāvatī there.
With a face like the full moon and a radiance like the moon’s crescent spreading forth,
she was like the night of the full moon remaining hidden out of fear of the dark fortnight.
She too, seeing him, rose up and honored him with various services, such as embracing his neck, which were appropriate for her long-standing longing.
Then, having been married by her according to the Gāndharva rite,
the prince remained there in secret with his beloved, his desires fulfilled.
After staying for several days, he spoke to his beloved at night:
"My friend, who has come along as my companion, is actually the son of a minister."
"And he remains here alone in the house of your elder sister;
O slender one, having gone there and paid him my respects, I shall return to your side."
Having heard that, the cunning Padmāvatī said to her beloved:
"Ah, noble son, I wish to ask you about those signs which were made by me."
"What did that friend, the minister’s son, say to you?
To her who had spoken thus, the prince replied:
"Nothing of that was known by me; but having learned everything, it was explained to me by that son of a minister, who is endowed with divine wisdom."
Having heard this and reflected upon it, that beautiful woman said to him:
"In that case, you have acted improperly, since you spoke of him to me only after such a long time."
"He who is your brother and friend is mine as well; indeed, I must always first offer him the customary hospitality of betel and other refreshments."
When she had spoken thus, he was granted leave by her; then, at night, the king’s son went by the same path as before to the presence of his friend.
And in the midst of their conversation, he related to him that account concerning his beloved,
which he had previously told in her presence regarding the naming and recognition of signs.
But that minister’s son did not believe him, thinking it improper;
meanwhile, the night there turned into dawn for those two.
Then, while the two of them were engaged in conversation after their evening rituals had concluded,
a friend of Padmāvatī arrived, carrying cooked food and betel in her hands.
Having inquired after the welfare of the minister’s son and provided him with hospitality,
she skillfully sought to prevent the prince from eating there.
In the course of conversation, having informed his mistress— who was awaiting his arrival for her meal and other affairs— that he had departed, he then left secretly from that place in an instant.
Then that minister’s son spoke to the prince:
"O King, behold a single marvel; I shall now show it to you."
Having said this, he then gave a single morsel of cooked food to a dog;
and having eaten it, the dog immediately perished.
Seeing that, the prince asked the minister's son, "What is this wonder? and he replied to him.
Having recognized me as a rogue through her knowledge of signs,
she, being devoted to you, sent me poisoned food with the desire to kill me.
"If he remains here, this prince will become focused solely on me;
but under my influence, he might abandon me and return to his own city."
Therefore, abandon your anger toward this woman;
because of her abandonment of her kin, you should devise a plan for her abduction—considering which, I shall tell it to you.
When the minister’s son had spoken thus, the prince there praised him, saying,
"It is true that you possess both wisdom and a noble character."
Unexpectedly, there arose outside the clamor of people overwhelmed by grief;
"Alas! Woe! The young son of the king has perished!"—thus was it heard.
Delighted upon hearing this, the minister’s son then said to the prince:
"Come now, let us go tonight to the house of Padmāvatī."
There, one should make her drink it until, from the intoxication of the drink,
she becomes unconscious, devoid of movement, and as if lifeless.
Then, while she was asleep, he marked her hip with a spear heated by fire and took away her collection of ornaments.
"You should come through the window, having descended by means of a hanging rope;
thereafter, I shall know how to ensure that all goes well."
Having said this and having had one fashioned with a tip resembling the bristles of a boar,
the minister’s son gave that trident to the prince.
The prince took that curved and harsh thing in his hand—
firm black iron, like the hearts of the beloved and her friend.
"So be it," he replied as before, and went to Padmāvatī’s house that night;
for the word of one's own minister, even if pure, is not to be questioned by masters.
There, having stripped her of her ornaments and marked her on the hips with a brand while she lay motionless from drink,
he went into the presence of his friend.
Having displayed his ornaments, he related to him exactly what had been done;
then that minister’s son also considered his desire accomplished.
Having gone to the cremation ground at dawn, he assumed the garb of an ascetic and freely made that prince his disciple.
And he said to him, "Go alone from here, taking this pearl necklace as if to sell it in the marketplace."
And he should speak of her as being of great value, so that no one at all would take her while she was being led about,
yet everyone who saw her would [be captivated].
If the city guards should seize you there, you must say without agitation: "My teacher gave this to me for the purpose of selling it. SoKss_12,8.165 (Vet_1.107) //
Thus dispatched by him, the prince then went and stood in the marketplace, wandering about while clearly wearing a string of pearls.
And being such as he was, he was seized by the city guards, who were searching for thieves at the command of the ivory-carver’s daughter, upon seeing him.
And at that very moment, he was led by them into the presence of the city magistrate;
and seeing him in the guise of an ascetic, the magistrate questioned him with gentleness.
“O Blessed One, from where did you obtain this pearl necklace that was lost here?
For the jewelry of the ivory-carver’s daughter was stolen during the night.”
Having heard that, the prince, who was in the guise of an ascetic, said to him:
"She was given to me by my preceptor; let her be approached and questioned."
Then the lord of the city approached him, bowed, and asked:
"O Blessed One, from where did you obtain this pearl necklace that has come into the hands of your disciple?"
Having heard this, that rogue made the place secluded and said to him:
"I am an ascetic who wanders constantly here and there through the forests."
Thus, having arrived here by fate, I remained in this cremation ground during the night and saw a circle of yoginīs assembled here and there.
And in their midst, a certain Yoginī of the Single Vehicle opened the lotus of the prince’s heart and offered him to Bhairava.
And that great illusionist, intoxicated by drink, began to snatch away my rosary as I was chanting, making contortions with her face.
And in my anger, I struck her excessively on the hip with a trident whose points were set ablaze by mantras.
"This pearl necklace was taken by me from her neck at that time;
it is that very one which, being unsuitable for an ascetic, is now for sale to me."
Having heard this, the city superintendent went and informed the king;
the king, too, having listened to that and having learned of her and that pearl necklace, [acted accordingly].
And having heard from the mouth of a trusted elderly woman sent to observe her— that she truly possessed that very mark of the "dart" on her hips— he was struck with longing.
Having reached the firm conclusion that "my son has been seized by that ḍākinī," he went in person to the presence of the ascetic, the minister’s son.
And having questioned her regarding the punishment for Padmāvatī, he, at her word,
ordered her banishment from the city while she was being mourned by her parents.
Though she was exiled and dwelling in the forest, she did not abandon her body even in her distress,
for she had conceived a plan with the minister’s son, which was carried out accordingly.
At the end of the day, as she was grieving, the minister’s son and the king’s son approached her on horseback, having discarded their ascetic garb.
Having comforted her and placed her upon a horse, they led her back to their own kingdom;
there the prince dwelt with her in contentment.
But the ivory-carver, believing his daughter had been devoured by carnivorous beasts in the forest, perished of grief; and his wife followed after him.
Having spoken thus, the Vetāla said again to the king:
"Sever this doubt of mine regarding which of these two, husband and wife, is guilty by reason of their murder."
"What sin has the minister's son committed, or what indeed has the prince done, or what has Padmāvatī? For you are the best among the wise."
And if, O King, knowing this, you do not speak the truth to me,
then this head of yours will certainly burst asunder into a hundred pieces.
When the Vetāla had spoken thus, King Trivikramasena, recognizing him and fearing the curse, replied to him in this way:
"O Lord of Yoga, what is there not to be known? For this is no sin on the part of these three; rather, that evil belongs to King Karṇotpala."
The Vetāla also said: "O King, what indeed is the fault of those three who did that?
What offense do the crows commit when the rice has been eaten by the swans?"
Then the king said to him, "None of those three are at fault;
for that was the business of the master, and thus it is blameless for the minister's son."
For those two, Prince Padmāvatī and the prince, were scorched by the fire of the arrows of desire; they were beyond reproach, faultless, and intent upon their own purpose.
But that King Karṇotpala, untrained in the treatises on political ethics,
did not investigate the purity of his own subjects through spies, even among his own kin.
Not knowing the conduct of rogues and unskilled in interpreting gestures and other signs,
he incurred the guilt by acting so thoughtlessly.
Having heard this, when the king had duly broken his silence and offered his reply, the Vetāla—
who was within that human corpse— immediately departed elsewhere, beyond all conjecture, by the power of illusion, in order to test the king's firmness.
And that king, remaining unshaken, again made a firm resolve to recover him.
The Ninth Wave. Then King Trivikramasena went once more to the vicinity of that śiṃśapā tree in order to bring back the vetāla.
Having arrived there at night, as he looked about by the light of the funeral pyre,
he then saw that corpse fallen on the ground, groaning.
Then that lord of the earth, having placed the Vetāla residing within the corpse upon his shoulder,
proceeded silently and swiftly to bring him back.
Then, from his shoulder, the vetāla spoke again to that king:
"O King, you have fallen into this great and unworthy hardship."
Therefore, listen as I describe a story for your amusement:
there is a land-grant village named Brahmasthala on the banks of the Kālindī.
There lived a Brahmin named Agnisvāmin who had mastered the Vedas;
to him was born a daughter of exceeding beauty named Mandāravatī.
Having fashioned her, who possessed a fresh and priceless beauty,
the Creator surely came to loathe his own previous creation of the celestial nymphs.
And while she was in the bloom of youth, three young Brahmin sons, equal in all virtues, arrived there from Kānyakubja.
And each of them requested her for his own sake from her father,
who would not give her to another even at the cost of his own life.
But her father gave her not even to one among them, fearing the death of the other two; consequently, she remained there as a maiden.
And all three of them, their gazes fixed solely upon the moon of her face,
remained there day and night, adopting the vow of the cakora bird.
Then, due to the onset of a fever accompanied by a burning sensation that arose suddenly,
the maiden Mandāravatī, it is said, passed away.
Then those sons of the brahmin, overwhelmed with grief, took her—
who had been adorned with ornaments— and having carried her to the cremation ground, they consigned her to the fire.
And one among them, having constructed a small hut right there,
remained with a bed made of their ashes, subsisting on alms obtained without asking.
The second, taking her bones, went to the Bhāgīrathī;
the third, having become an ascetic, went to wander through other lands.
Wandering on, that ascetic reached a village named Vakrolaka;
there, as a guest, he entered the house of a certain brahmin.
While he, being thus honored, was about to begin eating there,
a certain child began to cry out.
When he did not desist even though being pacified, his wife, seized by anger, took him by the arm and threw him into the blazing fire.
As soon as it was thrown, that creature of delicate limbs was reduced to ashes;
seeing this, the ascetic guest, his hair standing on end with thrill, said:
"Alas! Woe is me! I have entered the abode of a Brahmarākṣasa.
Therefore, I shall not eat this food here now, for it is indeed embodied sin."
To him who was speaking thus, that householder said: "Behold the power of my mantra, perfected through recitation, which restores the dead to life."
Having spoken thus, he took that manuscript of mantras and, having recited them,
he scattered consecrated dust upon the ashes there.
Then that boy rose up, still alive and in that very same form;
thereafter, the brahmin ascetic, being satisfied, ate there.
Even though he was a householder, he placed that manuscript on a wall-bracket,
and having eaten, he went to bed there at night together with her.
While that householder was asleep, the ascetic, desiring the life of his beloved, rose up stealthily and apprehensively took hold of that manuscript.
Having taken it and departed from there, traveling day and night,
he eventually reached that cremation ground where his beloved had been burned.
And at that moment, he saw him arrive there for a second time—
the one who had gone to cast his bones into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Then he spoke to both of them— that [man] and that first one— who were lying there in her ashes, having built a small hut upon it.
"Let this hut be cleared away so that I may raise up my beloved from the ashes while she is still alive, by means of some power of mantras."
Having thus urged them with persistence and having overturned the small hut,
that brahmin ascetic opened it and read that little book.
Having consecrated the dust with a mantra, he threw it into the ashes;
thereupon, Mandāravatī rose up alive from that place.
Having emerged from the fire, that maiden then bore a body of even greater luster than before,
as if it were fashioned out of gold.
Seeing her born again in such a form, all three of them became afflicted by love; desiring to possess her, they thus engaged in a mutual quarrel.
One said, "This wife was won by me through the power of mantras," and another said,
"This wife was obtained by me through the power of sacred fords."
"Since I have preserved this woman here by means of my ascetic heat and her ashes,
she is my wife"— thus he spoke as the third in this matter.
O Lord of the Earth, regarding the resolution of this dispute, please tell me your decision: to which of these two does this maiden rightfully become a wife?
"Your head shall split asunder if you know and do not speak," having heard this from the vetāla, the king replied to him thus:
He who, even after experiencing affliction, restored her to life by means of a mantra—
he was her father because he performed that act for her, but not her husband.
He who carried him to the Ganges is considered his son;
but he who remained performing austerities while embracing that bed of ashes was [the other].
It is in the cremation ground alone that he is called her husband out of affection;
for by him, who was deeply enamored, a fitting deed was indeed performed.
Having heard this from King Trivikramasena, who had thus broken his silence,
the Vetāla left his shoulder unexpectedly and returned to his own place.
Then the king, intent upon the goal for the sake of the mendicants,
again set his mind upon attaining it;
for one does not abandon a purpose once undertaken, even at the cost of one's life.
Those of firm resolve do not remain without having carried out their task.
